records.title: Scotland Against Spin
records.bodyText:
Campaigners in the Scottish Borders say windfarm applications should come under the same scrutiny as data centres.
The call comes after a key debate in the Scottish parliament in which Hannah Mary Goodlad, Minister for Public Finance, accepted an amendment put forward by Scottish Labour, that planning guidance for data centres “must provide clarity on spatial, community and social impacts of any such developments and that decisions must be based on community consent.”
Campaigners say the impact of windfarms and vast battery storage sites is equally damaging and should also be based on community consent, particularly given that Scotland’s energy needs have already been met.

records.bodyText:
On a wander through the back roads of the Planning Inspectorate, one of our supporters came across an interesting email.
The background to this is that a huge solar farm on the Cambridgeshire/Suffolk border, the Sunnica Energy Farm, which is a Nationally Significant Infrastructure Project (NSIP), was granted a Development Consent Order (DCO) by Ed Miliband in July 2024. The project covers three sites spanning 2,500 acres/ 1012 ha and would affect the villages of West Row and Mildenhall, Worlington and an area off the A14 near Newmarket. So far no construction has taken place.
On 8 April 2024, Claire Coutinho, at the time the Secretary of State for Energy Security and Net Zero, received an email with the subject 'Large DCO Appicayions ˜ Sunnica etc' (sic).
Coutinho's correspondent was writing 'to vehemently object' to the Sunnica proposal.
They wrote: 'Siting compounds and solar sites between and close to a number of closely related historic villages cause significant and detrimental industrialisation of a wholly rural area.'
Furthermore, they maintain that 'the development would, due to its location and scale, result in significant long-term harm to the character of the landscape including the setting of settlements.'
They go on to say that 'due to its location and scale, (the site) would fail to protect, conserve or enhance space between settlements and their wider landscape setting, key views into and out of settlements and the unspoiled nature and tranquillity of the area.'
The email was forwarded to the Department for Business, Energy and Industrial Strategy and was flagged as *Not a constituent*
Who could this person possibly be?
Why, none other than 'Christopher D G Wilson, Executive Chairman Worldwide Renewable Energy Global Ltd' (and founder of Calderdale Wind Farm Ltd).
I don't know precisely why Wilson got caught up in the campaign against Sunnica, but I suspect that, like his friend Richard Bannister, he is a racing man and may well be acquainted with the racing community around the Sunnica sites.
Let us hope that his concerns for the fate of the landscape around Sunnica also apply to our wholly rural moor, with its historic villages such as Haworth and its key views...
Just in case you were wondering what our campaign was doing at the time Wilson was firing off emails about his deep concerns for the environment, here's a lovely blog, published on 4 April 2024 and written by our supporter, the writer and cartographer Chris Goddard: https://markavery.info/.../guest-blog-walshaw-turbine-34.../

records.title: Environmentalists Against Wind Turbines
records.bodyText:
ORSTED HIRED COAST GUARD EXECUTIVE 6 MONTHS AFTER F/V MISTRESS ACCIDENT
August 2019
https://www.nationalfisherman.com/.../orsted-hires-coast...
The former Coast Guard waterways management chief for New England has joined offshore wind energy company Ørsted, as the emerging U.S. industry comes to grips with pushback from commercial fishermen and other interests.
Ed LeBlanc, a former Coast Guard officer and most recently chief of the Waterways Management Division for Coast Guard Sector Southeastern New England, will be manager of marine affairs for Ørsted U.S. Offshore Wind, the Denmark-based energy company’s American division.
In his last position of 16 years with the Coast Guard First District, LeBlanc was in the forefront of planning to how the newly arriving offshore wind industry could coexist with commercial fishing and maritime transportation traffic in the Northeast. An element of that will be safe vessel transit lanes through planned wind turbine arrays off Martha’s Vineyard, Mass.
Ed LeBlanc, the former chief of waterways management at the Coast Guard Southeast New England sector, is Ørsted's new manager of marine affairs.
LinkedIn photo.
https://www.linkedin.com/in/edward-leblanc-59492122/...
One conceptual layout proposed in late 2018 by the Responsible Offshore Development Alliance, a coalition of fishing groups, would set aside lanes with setbacks so fishing vessels can safely transit between ports like New Bedford, Mass., to Georges Bank and other fishing grounds.
The spacing and orientation of the turbine arrays is under intense debate, with commercial fishing groups in New England and New York warning the designs could make mobile gear fishing impossible.
The decision appears to be a sudden slowdown in what has been strong federal support for developing offshore wind. Democratic and Republican lawmakers from Massachusetts and Louisiana – both states that stand to gain jobs from building and operating the new offshore industry – wrote to Bernhardt and Secretary of Commerce Wilbur Ross Aug. 16 urging “your departments to work together to find a solution that will address concerns raised by stakeholders, protect the environment, and allow the Vineyard Wind project to remain viable.”
Signed by Sens. Ed Markey and Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts and Bill Cassidy and John Kennedy of Louisiana, the letter makes the case that offshore wind power will benefit Massachusetts residents with reliable energy – and Gulf of Mexico states, where the prospect of building turbine foundations and offshore wind service vessels is a bright hope for the maritime industry. Reps. Joseph Kennedy III, Richard Neal, and William Keating of Massachusetts and Steve Scalise of Louisiana also signed on to the message.
The members of Congress wrote that “Louisiana and Gulf Coast companies that have decades of experience working in the Gulf of Mexico are eager to make needed investments to support this project and future offshore wind energy projects.”
For Ørsted, adding LeBlanc, with his 40 years' experience with the Coast Guard, to its team is part of a push to build relationships with the larger maritime community.
“We are thrilled to add such an accomplished veteran of the USCG to our team. Ed’s breadth of experience will be a significant addition to the Marine Affairs department,” said John O’Keeffe, head of marine affairs U.S. for Ørsted, in announcing LeBlanc’s move.
LeBlanc has "invaluable institutional knowledge of how the offshore wind industry interacts with the marine community,” according to the Ørsted statement. “His experience working with industry since its nascency in the U.S. mirrors Ørsted’s own experience with the industry’s beginnings in Europe.”
The company says it “will bolster its marine community outreach efforts as its projects move closer to the construction phase. Ørsted’s commitment to working with the marine community, including the fishing industry, demonstrates how it has successfully built offshore wind farms across Europe to deliver clean energy and economic development to local communities.”
Ørsted is holding three of those community outreach sessions in New Jersey next week to talk about its proposed Ocean Wind project off Atlantic City. The first will be held Aug. 26 at 6 p.m. in the Stockton University Atlantic City Academic Center, located at 3711 Atlantic Avenue, Atlantic City.
In addition to the company’s outreach campaign, LeBlanc will help coordinate the company’s safety operations with the Coast Guard, and aim to establish industry-wide standards. That is a critical area for the service’s vessel and aviation operators, who must train to safely transit and conduct search and rescue operations amid turbine arrays.
The Coast Guard recently conducted its first-ever such exercise working with Ørsted and General Electric at the Block Island Wind Farm off Rhode Island.
That five-turbine, 30 MW array is the first U.S. commercial offshore wind pilot project – and a fraction of the size proposed for energy developments on offshore federal leases.
Kirk Moore
Senior Associate Editor

The National Grid is preparing us all for power cuts and spend £50 million a day balancing the grid … we’ve been close to national blackouts on many occasions in the last few years and adding more unreliable renewables would worsen it.
‘They’ KNOW SMR’s are coming, and by the time Wales got its 800 odd planned turbines they’d already be obsolete. Late 2020’s-early 2030s being estimated.
The scaremongering on so-called safety issues when it comes to small nuclear is palpable and myth-driven. Any half decent physicist will agree.
And if 1kg of uranium produces the same amount of energy as 3 million tonnes of coal (coal being used to produce turbines and solar panels) there really is no argument.
We must pressure Plaid Cymru to JUSTIFY wrecking the landscapes of Wales forever when better alternatives are not far away. There would then be no justification at all

records.title: Our Power
records.bodyText:
There’s been a lot of splashy coverage about Galileo Empower’s plan to use "AI technology" to cover energy bills for nearby residents around the Dorenell Wind Farm extension near Dufftown and the Cabrach.
It sounds like a win on the surface. Who wouldn't want £0 at the bottom of their energy bill?
But let’s look past the slick PR campaign.
A £1.8 million annual fund and automated bill credits are corporate handouts, designed to secure planning consent while external developers and global financial funds siphon off tens of millions of pounds in long-term profits generated right here on Moray’s hills.
Here is why rural communities across Scotland deserve better:
Discretionary Handouts vs. Equity: Industry data shows that 100% community-owned wind farms return up to 52 times more revenue to local areas than corporate community benefit schemes.
Zero Real Control: An AI-managed discount scheme keeps local residents completely dependent on the corporation's terms. If energy price caps shift, tax laws change, or the asset is sold, those "handouts" can disappear.
True Local Investment: When a community owns its energy assets, the profits don't go to foreign shareholders, they stay 100% local to build affordable council housing, fund school retention, upgrade rural transport, and guarantee low-cost power permanently.
Moray’s land, wind, and landscape are priceless local assets. We shouldn't be settling for crumbs dropped off the bottom of a corporate balance sheet.
It’s time to shift the conversation in Scotland from "How much discount will you give us?" to "Why shouldn't the community own the energy?" 
 What do you think? Would you prefer a monthly bill credit from a multinational firm, or full community equity and ownership of local wind farms? Let’s hear your thoughts below.

records.title: Our Power
records.bodyText:
Another very busy day at conference, with plenty of opportunities to get around the exhibition stands, meet organisations and discuss issues affecting people across the constituency.
I was pleased to meet with RNIB Scotland and hear more about the issues affecting blind and partially sighted people, and the work they are doing to improve accessibility and support.
I also stopped by the MCS Foundation stand, where they had put together a Cowdenbeath-specific quiz as part of their snakes and ladders game on heat pumps and energy efficiency. It was a good way of highlighting just how far we still have to go in improving energy efficiency, moving towards cleaner heating and helping to bring down energy costs for households across the constituency.
I met with Our Power to discuss community ownership of energy assets and the potential benefits that could bring locally, and also visited the Movember stand to learn more about their work supporting men’s mental health and wellbeing, alongside their long-standing work raising awareness of prostate cancer and other men’s health issues. They even managed to get me into the barber’s chair for a quick tidy-up before the rest of conference!
A really useful conversation with StepChange focused on the support available to people experiencing debt and the importance of people getting help as early as possible. I’ll be making sure information about their services is available through my constituency office so that people know where they can turn for free and practical support.
I also learned more about the Bank of Scotland Foundation and the important core funding it provides to charities and community organisations across Scotland.
Alongside the exhibition, I joined a number of fringe events and had the opportunity to sit down with Forth Ports for further discussions about the Rosyth ferry and their decision to withdraw from the service. I also spoke with Scottish Swimming about community access to facilities in Inverkeithing and what the future may hold there.
It was an extremely busy day, but a very productive one, with plenty of useful conversations and a number of follow-ups now to take forward after conference.

records.title: Scottish Electricity Generating Stations
records.bodyText:
Methil Power Station
As part of an agreement with the National Coal Board (NCB), the South of Scotland Electricity Board (SSEB) took control of Kelty Power Station and agreed to build power plants capable of burning coal slurry. This slurry was a waste product from coal washeries located across the central belt of Scotland. As a result new power stations were constructed at Barony and Methil in 1960s.
Methil Power Station was situated in the town of Methil at Innerleven on the south bank of the River Leven on the Firth of Forth,
The plant was designed by Ross-Smith and Jamieson Architects and was built on an area of reclaimed land which was leased from Forth Ports plc.
The plant was a coal-slurry fired power station which utilised local Fife coalfield waste from coal washeries and had a total capacity 57 MWe output. It was a ‘sister’ station to the generating station of Barony in Ayrshire and was commissioned in 1965. It was finally closed in 1999 and demolition began in early 2010.
The site included the following elements:
Rail network - bringing in coal slurry to the east side of the main building.
Coal handling and crane gantry areas - the trains reversed into the gantry area where there were coal grabs. The coal would be emptied into concrete open ‘bund’ which was used as the coal slurry store. This would then be transferred by crane to the Milling Area bay into individual hoppers above each hammer mill.
Milling Area – where coal slurry was pulverised in hammer mill pulverisers (into a finer uniform powder) and dried by the hot air from the boiler furnace.
Boiler House – where the coal dust was blown into the boilers by fans. There was one boiler for each turbine. The coal dust would then be burnt, and water was heated to produce steam to drive the turbo alternator. Make water was stored in blue tanks on site and taken from the mains supply before treatment for use in the process.
Turbine Hall: the electricity was produced by the turbo alternators and supplied via transformers (stepped up to 33,000 volts) and then onto a substation connected to the National Grid.
Turbine Hall 2 x 30MWe English Electric Turbo Alternators and condensers and associated auxiliary equipment. Various administrative buildings and workshops and the best canteen in the SSEB
Electrical annexe - housed the transformers and switchgear.
Chimney – Methil had one brick (single flue) chimney, clad in concrete. This removed fuel gases from the process to atmosphere.
Precipitators – They removed dust from the flue gases and consisted of large, cladded, steel boxes with HV electrodes to charge the dust particles to collector plants. ID fans which draw the flue gases from the boiler and discharged@ to the chimney. Most precipitates were gathered in hoppers and removed from the site with the ash from the boilers.
Water Treatment – for treating mains water used to top up the process cycle.
Cooling Water Intake & Outfall. Seawater extracted from the Forth to feed condensers and discharged waste heat back to the Forth. The condenser cools steam leaving the turbine, back into water to allow reuse in the process cycle. Unfortunately the CW inlet was located close to the regional sewage discharge outlet...
The power station consisted of two 30MW English Electric Turbo Alternator generation units for a peak output of 57 MWe the station. It was commissioned in 1965 for the then South of Scotland Electricity Board. Built on the site of a golf course, it was designed to utilise low-grade coal slurry supplied from the washeries of the nearby Fife coalfield. This coal was delivered by road and rail wagons shunted into and out of elevated sidings. Like almost all other coal-fired power stations in Scotland, Methil did not use cooling towers, instead using sea water as coolant.
As the Scottish coalfields were exhausted or abandoned in the mid-1980s, waste accumulated in coal tips (bings), and this waste was used as a fuel in the Methil and Barony power stations. However, as the tips were cleared, operations at the two stations ceased due to lack of coal-slurry fuel and the uneconomical operation of smaller power stations.
The station ceased generating in 2000 and was put into standby as a strategic reserve. The power station was finally demolished in 2011 as part of a regeneration of this area.
The site was transferred back to Forth Ports plc after the site had been cleared.
— in Methil, Fife.

records.bodyText:
CHAPELLCROSS: WHAT HAPPENED TO THE WIDER VISION, AND WHERE HAS THE PUBLIC MONEY GONE?
The earlier proposals for Chapelcross described a mixed-use employment, energy and innovation site.
The council’s May 2021 programme update included five themes:
• Green energy and net-zero industry.
• Sustainable agriculture, aquaculture and food.
• Clean mobility and logistics.
• Education, skills and training.
• Digital connectivity and data services.
The 2024 masterplan developed that wider approach through hydrogen, green industry, enterprise and energy campuses. It included flexible premises for smaller businesses, manufacturing and supply-chain activity.
Digital infrastructure was already part of the earlier vision. The question is how a development now dominated by hyperscale data centres delivers the wider economic and community benefits originally envisaged? And isn’t just a sudden jump onto the Data Centre bandwagon and a money grab!
Their ongoing use on this public funding now needs a clear explanation. Not the least because what’s now planned is substantially different from what received public funding.
Publicly available and published records show:
• A May 2021 report confirmed a £134,000 NDA payment to Dumfries and Galloway Council under a five-year £495,000 Chapelcross grant agreement.
• A SOSE freedom-of-information response recorded a grant of up to £150,000 over three years from 2022/23 to support the council’s Chapelcross business-case work.
• The council’s November 2024 report identified £15.3 million of proposed government funding through Borderlands, plus £5.5 million committed by the council, for roads and services to unlock the site.
• The Ferret reported this month that the Borderlands allocation was up to £17.3 million. Both Borderlands and the council told it that funding had not yet been awarded and remained conditional.
Now all these figures concern different dates, purposes and funding stages. And so they cannot simply be added together or described as money handed to CX Tech that’s now due to be handed back etc. 
But since the attendees at the first (and only?) public meeting reported that the CX representative stated “hat money would have to be paid back if the site is not developed” it might seem important that the council, Scottish and UK governments and the public get any relevant written explanations.
Questions that now seem important and need a clear legal answer include:
Which organisation received the money, how much, and when?
Which agreement or agreements now contain the repayment requirements?
What precisely triggers any repayment, and by what deadline?
Does any of this require this particular data centre scheme, does this change of plan now invalidate the original funding plan that was far more community oriented?
Could another suitable development meet the conditions of this hyperscale data centre does not?
Which elements of the earlier mixed-use vision remain, and where will they be delivered?
Does ANY of the original bison remain among thes enemies plans?
I remember seeing the original plans and how it was about regenerating a genuinely brownfield site to get some use for the local community and businesses. Not the current exploitative land and cash grab for the usual suspects. 
Please Google and look for the following documents yourself (perhaps the Green Party for example has the manpower and volunteers to dive deeply into this?):
“CX SSG Mark Fulton CX programme May21”
“Chapelcross Development Framework November 2024”
“Chapelcross council 5 November 2024 15.3 5.5”
“SOSE 127 FOI Chapelcross April 2024”
“Chapelcross Ferret October 2026 public funds”
I think we need to call on the council, all funding bodies and both governments to now examine and publish (any not available) the funding agreements, payments to date and repayment conditions for the site, CX and all stakeholders. 
The community and tax payers should be able to see exactly what has been funded and what obligations follow.
